Itô process (Xt​=X0​+∫0t​bs​ds+∫0t​σs​dWs​)

Words: 66
Stochastic calculus OurBigBook.com
An Itô process is a continuous semimartingale expressible as the displayed sum, with adapted coefficients locally integrable for the time integral and locally square integrable for the Itô integral. The coefficients may depend on the whole past; an Itô diffusion usually specifies them as functions of the current state and time. A continuously differentiable deterministic process is an Itô process with zero Brownian coefficient. The Itô formula and Itô product rule apply to these processes.

Stochastic Fubini theorem (∫du∫H(s,u)dWs​=∫(∫H(s,u)du)dWs​)

Words: 40
Stochastic calculus OurBigBook.com
A theorem interchanging a parameter integral with an Itô integral, under appropriate measurability and integrability hypotheses. For a bounded deterministic integrand on a finite parameter-time rectangle, the square-integrability conditions hold; triangular domains can be handled by an indicator of the domain.

Semimartingale

Words: 599 Articles: 10
Stochastic calculus OurBigBook.com
A semimartingale is the sum of a local martingale and an adapted finite-variation process. This is the broad class of integrators for which the Itô stochastic integral is defined.

Continuous semimartingale

Words: 38
Semimartingale OurBigBook.com
A continuous semimartingale is a continuous adapted process admitting a decomposition X=X0​+N+V, with N a zero-starting continuous local martingale and V continuous adapted finite variation. The decomposition is unique because a continuous finite-variation local martingale starting at zero vanishes. Its quadratic variation is [X]=[N].

Semimartingale stability under an absolutely continuous measure change

Words: 185 Articles: 1
Semimartingale OurBigBook.com
If X is a semimartingale under P and Q≪P, then it is a semimartingale under Q. The Bichteler-Dellacherie theorem gives a short proof: terminal elementary integrals associated with uniformly small elementary predictable processes with stopping-time intervals converge to zero in P-probability. Uniform convergence on compacts in probability under an absolutely continuous measure change, or its single-random-variable proof, transfers convergence to Q. The same good-integrator characterization now applies under Q. Adaptedness and càdlàg paths are preserved because P-null sets remain Q-null; if necessary use the usual Q-completion of the same filtration. If the integrands are bounded only outside Q-null sets, clip their coefficients to the specified deterministic bounds before applying the P-criterion; this preserves their Q-versions. Completion adds only equivalent versions of measurable coefficients. This theorem does not preserve the local martingale property.

Stochastic integral under an absolutely continuous measure change

Words: 64
Semimartingale stability under an absolutely continuous measure change OurBigBook.com
If Q≪P and X is a semimartingale under both measures, the two integrals of any locally bounded predictable H against X agree up to Q-indistinguishability. Elementary integrals are the same increment sums. Bounded pointwise convergence of integrands, stochastic dominated convergence, and transfer of probability convergence from P to Q extend equality by the monotone-class theorem. Localize to remove boundedness.

Bichteler-Dellacherie theorem

Words: 78
Semimartingale OurBigBook.com
An adapted càdlàg process is a semimartingale exactly when it is a good integrator: on each finite horizon, for every sequence of bounded elementary predictable processes with stopping-time intervals Hn whose deterministic uniform bounds tend to zero, the elementary terminal integrals (Hn⋅X)T​ tend to zero in probability. The elementary integral is a finite sum of measurable coefficients times subsequent increments; the characterization says precisely when this operation extends continuously to stochastic integration. The theorem is used here as a standard characterization, not proved from first principles.

Finite-variation process

Words: 153 Articles: 2
Semimartingale OurBigBook.com
A process A has finite variation on compact intervals when every sample path has finite total variation of a function there. Such a process can be integrated pathwise by the Lebesgue-Stieltjes integral.

Total-variation process (Vt​(A))

Words: 126 Articles: 1
Finite-variation process OurBigBook.com
For a path of finite variation, its total-variation process is
Vt​(A)=supπ​∑[u,v]∈π​∣Av​−Au​∣,
(1)
where the supremum is over every partition of an interval of [0,t]. It is an increasing process, and the signed measure dA satisfies ∣dA∣=dV(A).
Càdlàg regularity of finite total variation (ΔVt​=∣ΔXt​∣(t>0))
Words: 95
Total-variation process OurBigBook.com
If a càdlàg function has finite variation on compact intervals, its total-variation process is finite, nondecreasing, and càdlàg. Left limits follow from monotonicity. For right continuity, approximate the variation on [t,s] by one finite partition. Changing its first endpoint from t to u↓t changes the sum by at most ∣Xu​−Xt​∣, which tends to zero. Additivity of variation then bounds V(u)−V(t) by an arbitrarily small error. Its jump is the absolute jump of X. Without locally finite variation, right continuity can fail even as an extended-valued assertion: Xt​=tsin(1/t) with X0​=0 has infinite variation on every interval starting at zero.

Semimartingale decomposition

Words: 118 Articles: 2
Semimartingale OurBigBook.com
A semimartingale has a decomposition X=X0​+M+A into a local martingale M and an adapted finite-variation process A. Under standard normalizations the decomposition is unique.

Continuous semimartingale decomposition

Words: 97 Articles: 1
Semimartingale decomposition OurBigBook.com
A continuous semimartingale has a decomposition in which both the local-martingale and finite-variation parts are continuous.
Initial-value integrability in normalized semimartingale decompositions (X=M+A,A0​=0 ⟹ M0​=X0​)
Words: 81
Continuous semimartingale decomposition OurBigBook.com
With the local martingale definition requiring each stopped process itself to be a martingale, the initial value is integrable. A normalized continuous semimartingale decomposition X=M+A with A0​=0 can therefore have a local-martingale part only if X0​ is integrable. A smooth transformation need not preserve this condition: take M=0, At​=G for an initially known standard normal random variable, and f(x,a)=ea2. Then f(M0​,A0​) is finite almost surely but has infinite expectation. The always-valid decomposition is instead X=X0​+N+V with a zero-starting continuous local martingale N and a continuous finite-variation process V starting at zero.

Quadratic variation ([X]t​)

Words: 1k Articles: 24
Stochastic calculus OurBigBook.com
The quadratic variation of a continuous semimartingale is the limit in probability
[X]t​=lim∣π∣→0​∑[u,v]∈π​(Xv​−Xu​)2.
(2)
Finite-variation processes have zero quadratic variation, while a Brownian motion satisfies [B]t​=t.

Predictable quadratic variation (⟨M⟩)

Words: 61
Quadratic variation OurBigBook.com
For a zero-starting square-integrable martingale, the predictable quadratic variation is the predictable increasing process A for which M2−A is a martingale. For a compensated jump process it integrates squared jump sizes against their rates. Unlike optional quadratic variation, it need not equal the sum of squared realized jumps. For continuous local martingales, the two brackets coincide after localization.

Uniqueness of an increasing square compensator (M2−A local martingale,A0​=0)

Words: 50
Quadratic variation OurBigBook.com
For a continuous local martingale M, at most one continuous adapted increasing process A starting at zero makes M2−A a local martingale. The difference of two candidates is a continuous finite-variation process and a local martingale, hence constant; its initial value is zero. Without the initial-value normalization only uniqueness up to an initial constant is possible.

Dyadic quadratic variation of a bounded continuous martingale (Esupt≤1​∣At(n)​−At(m)​∣2→0)

Words: 91
Quadratic variation OurBigBook.com
Let X be a continuous martingale on [0,1] with X0​=0 and ∣Xt​∣≤C. For the dyadic squared-increment sums, including the unfinished increment at time t, set At(n)​=∑k​(Xk2−n∧t​−X(k−1)2−n∧t​)2. The associated martingale transform Mt(n)​=(Xt2​−At(n)​)/2 satisfies E(M1(n)​)2≤C4 and E(A1(n)​)2≤10C4. Discrete martingale orthogonality, the path modulus of continuity and the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality show that the terminal transforms are Cauchy in L2. The Doob L2 maximal inequality then gives Esupt≤1​∣At(n)​−At(m)​∣2→0. The sums need not be increasing in time before taking the limit. This provides an elementary construction of quadratic variation under boundedness.

Finite-variation terms do not change quadratic variation ([M+A]=[M](A continuous of finite variation))

Words: 59
Quadratic variation OurBigBook.com
On a compact interval, squared increments of a continuous finite variation process are bounded by its modulus of continuity at the mesh size times its total variation, and therefore vanish. The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality bounds the mixed increment sum by the square root of the product of the two squared-increment sums. The local-martingale sum is bounded in probability, so the mixed term also vanishes.

Localization and patching of quadratic variation

Words: 59
Quadratic variation OurBigBook.com
Stop a continuous local martingale at increasing level-and-time stopping times to obtain bounded martingales. Their limits of discrete quadratic variation sums agree before the earlier stopping time, because the sums commute exactly with stopping. These continuous limits patch into a continuous adapted nondecreasing process. On each compact interval, the chance that the stopping time occurs early tends to zero, giving uniform convergence on compacts in probability for the original sums.

Quadratic variation from completed grid increments (Sn​(t)=∑tkn​≤t​(Xtkn​​−Xtk−1n​​)2)

Words: 56
Quadratic variation OurBigBook.com
Completed squared increments form a nondecreasing step process. The continuous sum that includes the last partial increment differs by at most the square of the path's modulus of continuity over one mesh interval. Therefore both have the same limit in uniform convergence on compacts in probability. This proves monotonicity of the limiting quadratic variation without incorrectly asserting monotonicity of each continuous partial-increment sum.

Weighted realized variance (Λn​(g))

Words: 63 Articles: 1
Quadratic variation OurBigBook.com
For observations of an Itô integral on a partition of an interval, the statistic ∑i​g(ti−1​)(Xti​​−Xti−1​​)2 estimates ∫g(t)σ(t)2dt. With a deterministic noise coefficient the squared increments are independent, and the fluctuation has variance 2∑i​g(ti−1​)2(∫ti−1​ti​​σ2)2.

Spot variance (σ(t)2)

Words: 31
Weighted realized variance OurBigBook.com
The spot variance is the instantaneous squared noise coefficient σ(t)2 of an Itô integral. It can be estimated by averaging the weighted realized variance over a shrinking time window. A Hölder continuity assumption bounds the smoothing bias.

Quadratic variation obstruction to Hölder regularity (∑k=0N−1​(w((k+1)/N)−w(k/N))2≤C2N1−2α)

Words: 55
Quadratic variation OurBigBook.com
A function with finite Hölder seminorm of exponent α>1/2 has squared-increment sum on a uniform N-interval partition bounded by C2N1−2α, hence tending to zero. This conflicts with a nonzero quadratic-variation limit. In particular dyadic quadratic variation of Brownian motion prevents a Brownian coordinate law supported on such a Hölder space. This argument alone gives no conclusion at the critical exponent 1/2.

Dyadic quadratic variation of Brownian motion (E(Qn​−1)2=21−n)

Words: 49
Quadratic variation OurBigBook.com
On [0,1], the sum Qn​ of squared adjacent dyadic increments of standard Brownian motion has EQn​=1 and var(Qn​)=21−n. Therefore Qn​→1 in L2. On an interval of length t, scaling gives mean t and variance 2t22−n. Independence is used within each grid, not between different grids.

Dyadic power variation of a continuous local martingale (∑i​∣Δi​M∣p)

Words: 51
Quadratic variation OurBigBook.com
Along the dyadic partitions of an interval of [0,1], the sums ∑i​∣Δi​M∣p of a continuous local martingale tend to zero in probability for p>2. If 0<p<2 and these sums are eventually bounded almost surely, then M is constant on [0,1]: compare them with the sums defining quadratic variation, using the maximum increment, which tends to zero by uniform continuity.

[M,N]t​=lim∣π∣→0​∑[u,v]∈π​(Mv​−Mu​)(Nv​−Nu​).
(3)

Quadratic covariations of an analytic Brownian image ([U]t​=[V]t​=∫0t​∣f′(Zs​)∣2ds,[U,V]t​=0)

Words: 42
Quadratic covariation OurBigBook.com
For an analytic function f=u+iv and planar Brownian motion Z=X+iY with independent standard coordinates, the Cauchy-Riemann equations make u,v harmonic. The Itô formula gives dU=ux​dX+uy​dY and dV=−uy​dX+ux​dY. Localizing the derivatives proves both coordinates are local martingales. Squaring their diffusion coefficients and multiplying the two rows gives the displayed quadratic variations and zero quadratic covariation.

Covariance identity for continuous square-integrable martingales (E[Mt​Nt​]=E[M,N]t​)

Words: 33
Quadratic covariation OurBigBook.com
For two zero-starting continuous martingales square-integrable at time t, the Itô isometry gives E(Mt​±Nt​)2=E[M±N]t​. The polarization identity yields the displayed identity. Integrability of the cross-bracket follows from the Kunita-Watanabe inequality and the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.

Weakly orthogonal continuous martingales (E[Ms​Nt​]=0(s,t≥0))

Words: 49
Quadratic covariation OurBigBook.com
For zero-starting L2-bounded continuous martingales, this condition is equivalent to E[Mt​Nt​]=0 at equal times, by conditioning the later factor. The covariance identity for continuous square-integrable martingales also makes it equivalent to E[M,N]t​=0. It is weaker than the vanishing bracket condition for orthogonal continuous local martingales: Bt∧1​ and Bt∧12​−(t∧1) have zero equal-time covariance but nonzero bracket 2∫0t∧1​Bs​ds.

Orthogonal continuous local martingales ([M,N]=0)

Words: 144 Articles: 2
Quadratic covariation OurBigBook.com
Two continuous local martingales are orthogonal when their quadratic covariation is zero. With zero initial values, the martingale product identity says that their product is a local martingale. For two Brownian motions in a common filtration, orthogonality and the Lévy characterization of multidimensional Brownian motion make the pair a two-dimensional Brownian motion and imply independence. Merely having the two marginal Brownian motion laws on the same space does not imply orthogonality.
Knight theorem for orthogonal martingales (Mj​(t)=Bj​(⟨Mj​⟩t​))
Words: 42
Orthogonal continuous local martingales OurBigBook.com
Let M1​,…,MN​ be continuous local martingales starting at zero, with ⟨Mi​,Mj​⟩=0 for i=j and ⟨Mj​⟩∞​=∞ almost surely. The individual Dambis-Dubins-Schwarz theorem time changes produce independent standard Brownian motions Bj​ with Mj​(t)=Bj​(⟨Mj​⟩t​). Independence is between the Brownian motions; each may still depend on its own clock.
Complex exponential of two orthogonal Brownian motions (Mt​=eBt​+iϑt​)
Words: 52
Orthogonal continuous local martingales OurBigBook.com
For orthogonal continuous local martingales B,ϑ that are standard Brownian motions, the real part X=eBcosϑ and imaginary part Y=eBsinϑ are continuous local martingales. The Itô formula gives dX=XdB−Ydϑ and dY=YdB+Xdϑ, since the two diagonal second-order terms cancel. Their quadratic variations equal ∫0t​e2Bs​ds and their quadratic covariation is zero. If C=[B,ϑ] is nonzero, the omitted drift terms are respectively −YdC and XdC, so the orthogonality hypothesis is essential.

Quadratic covariation under an absolutely continuous measure change

Words: 121 Articles: 1
Quadratic covariation OurBigBook.com
For continuous semimartingales and Q≪P, their quadratic covariation has the same version under the two probability measures, up to Q-indistinguishability of stochastic processes. The dyadic product sums have the same limit by uniform convergence on compacts in probability under an absolutely continuous measure change. Uniqueness of a limit in probability identifies that limit with the bracket under Q. Semimartingale stability under an absolutely continuous measure change supplies the correct class under Q: a local martingale need not remain a local martingale. Taking the two processes equal proves the same statement for quadratic variation without a separate assumption.
Quadratic variation under an absolutely continuous measure change
Words: 50
Quadratic covariation under an absolutely continuous measure change OurBigBook.com
If Q≪P and a continuous semimartingale is a semimartingale under both measures, its quadratic variations agree Q-indistinguishably. The same squared-increment sums converge uniformly on compacts in probability under both measures: absolute continuity transfers the original convergence, and uniqueness of the limit identifies the two continuous versions. Equivalence of measures is unnecessary.

The Itô formula makes exp(iu⋅(Xt​−X0​)+∣u∣2t/2) a local martingale, whose deterministic modulus bound on bounded horizons makes it a true martingale. Its conditional expectation identifies every increment as centered Gaussian with covariance (t−s)I, independent of the past. This proves the converse via the Lévy characterization of multidimensional Brownian motion. The forward implication is the Itô formula.

Diffusion approximation theorem (nE(ΔXn∣x)→b(x),nE((ΔXn)2∣x)→a(x))

Words: 104
Martingale problem OurBigBook.com
For discrete-time Markov chains run at time step 1/n, suppose the displayed conditional moments converge uniformly on compact sets to continuous coefficients, the local conditional large-jump second moments vanish, initial laws converge, and compact containment holds on each finite horizon. If the limiting diffusion martingale problem is well-posed and nonexplosive, the chain laws converge to its solution. Vanishing jumps give a continuous limit; linearly interpolated paths converge in the uniform path topology and step paths in Skorokhod J1 topology. Local moment bounds give tightness after exit-time localization. Taylor expansion identifies the limiting test-function martingales, and uniqueness of the martingale problem makes every subsequential limit the same. The diffusion approximation of a birth-death process is an important example.

Well-posed martingale problem

Words: 66
Martingale problem OurBigBook.com
A martingale problem is well-posed for a specified test domain and class of paths if it admits a solution for every specified starting point and that solution is unique in law. Existence on one fixed probability space is not required. Test-domain and true-versus-local conventions must be stated. For bounded diffusion coefficients and Cb2​ test functions, boundedness on every finite horizon upgrades the local identities to true martingale identities.

Diffusion martingale problem (L=21​∑i,j​aij​∂ij​+∑i​bi​∂i​)

Words: 239 Articles: 3
Martingale problem OurBigBook.com
For bounded measurable a,b, with a symmetric positive semidefinite, an L-diffusion is a continuous adapted process X such that g(Xt​)−g(X0​)−∫0t​Lg(Xs​)ds is a true martingale for every g∈Cb2​. The general local martingale problem may instead use compactly supported test functions and require only a local martingale. Specify the test class and the true or local convention when coefficients are unbounded.
Bounded-domain harmonic uniqueness for a diffusion
Words: 57
Diffusion martingale problem OurBigBook.com
For a bounded-domain diffusion with almost surely finite exit time τD​, bounded L-harmonic functions continuous up to the boundary satisfy u(x)=Ex​u(XτD​​). Stop the test-function martingale and use bounded convergence. Identical boundary values therefore imply identical harmonic functions. Uniform ellipticity and bounded SDE coefficients ensure finite exit by the projection argument.

Projection unboundedness of a uniformly elliptic diffusion
Words: 58
Diffusion martingale problem OurBigBook.com
For an SDE with bounded drift and diffusion coefficients and ∑k​⟨ξ,σk​(x)⟩2≥λ∣ξ∣2, each fixed nonzero scalar projection of a solution is unbounded in absolute value almost surely. Rescale a slab to (−1,1); its projected drift is controlled by its uniformly positive bracket density. The exit with drift controlled by quadratic variation then forces exit from every slab in a countable exhaustion.
// Target: probability-and-statistics.bigb
Time-dependent test functions for a diffusion martingale problem (Mtf​=f(t,Xt​)−f(0,X0​)−∫0t​(∂s​+L)f(s,Xs​)ds)
Words: 68
Diffusion martingale problem OurBigBook.com
For an L-diffusion with bounded coefficients and f∈Cb1,2​, Mf is a continuous martingale. Freeze the time argument along a deterministic partition, apply the spatial martingale problem on each interval, and pass to the limit by the dominated convergence theorem. The same proof works if the absolute drift coefficients and the trace of the diffusivity have integrable time integrals along the path on every finite horizon. Local hypotheses alone give a local martingale conclusion.

E(X)t​=exp(Xt​−X0​−21​[X]t​).
(39)
It solves dZt​=Zt​dXt​ with Z0​=1.

Pathwise uniqueness for a multiplicative martingale equation (dZ=ZdM,Z0​=z>0⟹Zt​=zexp(Mt​−M0​−21​[M]t​))

Words: 44
Doléans-Dade exponential OurBigBook.com
The Itô formula gives dlogZ=dM−21​d[M] for a strictly positive solution. Therefore equal initial values give indistinguishable solutions. Conversely the displayed exponential satisfies the equation. This is uniqueness for a fixed continuous local martingale driver and does not require the exponential to be a true martingale.

Stochastic logarithm (L=∫Z−1dZ)

Words: 80 Articles: 1
Doléans-Dade exponential OurBigBook.com
For a strictly positive continuous semimartingale Z, its stochastic logarithm is ∫Z−1dZ. When Z is a continuous local martingale starting at one, this is a local martingale L and the Itô formula gives Z=exp(L−⟨L⟩/2). Unlike the ordinary logarithm, it has no compensating finite-variation term.

Divergent logarithmic clock for a positive local martingale tending to zero (Mt​→0 ⟹ ⟨X⟩∞​=∞)

Words: 33
Stochastic logarithm OurBigBook.com
Write a positive continuous local martingale as M=exp(X−⟨X⟩/2) using its stochastic logarithm. If Mt​→0, its logarithmic bracket must diverge. Otherwise the finite-bracket convergence lemma makes X converge finitely and the exponential has a positive limit.

Kazamaki's condition

Words: 40
Doléans-Dade exponential OurBigBook.com
This is an exponential-moment criterion for the stochastic exponential to be a true martingale. In the infinite-horizon stopped-moment form, a zero-starting convergent continuous local martingale satisfying supT​EeMT​/2<∞ has a uniformly integrable martingale E(M). The half-threshold for the exponential-martingale Hölder bound first controls strict scalings. The terminal scaling inequality for stochastic exponentials and terminal expectation criterion for a nonnegative local martingale then include the endpoint scaling.

Terminal scaling inequality for stochastic exponentials (EE(rX)∞​≥(EE(X)∞​)r2(EerX∞​/2)−2(r−1))

Doléans-Dade exponential OurBigBook.com
For a convergent continuous local martingale and r>1, factor E(X) into E(rX)1/r2 and an ordinary exponential. Apply the Holder inequality and then the concave Jensen inequality to the fractional power 2/(r+1). The displayed lower bound is informative when the terminal exponential moment is finite.

Hölder factorization of stochastic exponentials (C(p,q)=(pq−pq​)/(q−1))

Doléans-Dade exponential OurBigBook.com
For a zero-starting continuous local martingale X, the stochastic exponential satisfies
E(X)p=E(pq​X)1/q(eC(p,q)X)(q−1)/q.
(40)
The Holder inequality and the supermartingale property of the first exponential bound its stopped pth moment by (EeC(p,q)XT​)(q−1)/q. The subtraction in the coefficient is pq​−1, not a square root of pq−1.

Half-threshold for the exponential-martingale Hölder bound (infp,q>1​(pq−pq​)/(q−1)=1/2)

Hölder factorization of stochastic exponentials OurBigBook.com
For fixed q>1, the coefficient in the Hölder factorization of stochastic exponentials exceeds q​/(q​+1)>1/2. Taking q=1+ε and p=1+ε2 approaches one-half. Thus a uniform stopped exponential moment at coefficient one-half bounds some pth moment of each strict scaling E(aM), 0<a<1.

If a continuous local martingale M satisfies
Eexp(21​[M]T​)<∞,

Bounded-bracket criterion for a stochastic exponential ([M]∞​≤C)

Words: 36
Novikov's condition OurBigBook.com
For a zero-start continuous local martingale M with [M]∞​≤C deterministically, its stochastic exponential is a uniformly integrable martingale. For each p>1, supt​EE(M)tp​≤ep(p−1)C/2. Its terminal value is strictly positive, so it defines an equivalent infinite-horizon change of measure by the Girsanov theorem.

Dambis-Dubins-Schwarz proof of the Novikov condition

Words: 53
Novikov's condition OurBigBook.com
Write Mt​=B[M]t​​ by the Dambis-Dubins-Schwarz theorem and stop the exponential Brownian martingale when Bs​−s first reaches b<0. The stopped exponential has mean one. Its boundary contribution before [M]T​ is at most
ebEe[M]T​/2,
(42)
which vanishes as b→−∞. The remaining term converges monotonically to E(M)t​, proving that its expectation is one.

Girsanov theorem

Words: 666 Articles: 9
Doléans-Dade exponential OurBigBook.com
Girsanov's theorem describes how a change of probability measure changes the drift of a semimartingale. If the appropriate stochastic exponential is a true martingale, weighting by it turns Wt​+∫0t​θs​ds into a Brownian motion under the new measure.

Ornstein-Uhlenbeck likelihood relative to Wiener measure (Lt​=exp(−μ∫0t​ωs​dωs​−2μ2​∫0t​ωs2​ds))

Words: 70
Girsanov theorem OurBigBook.com
On each finite horizon the displayed Radon-Nikodym derivative changes Wiener measure into the law of dX=dB−μXdt. Stop at coordinate magnitude n so the Novikov condition applies. Under each stopped tilted measure the coordinate solves the drifted equation, and the Gronwall inequality with the Doob L2 maximal inequality bounds its maximal second moment uniformly in n. The probability of reaching n therefore tends to zero; this proves that the unstopped density has expectation one. No unrestricted large-time Novikov estimate is needed.

Bounded Girsanov density for exit of an unstable linear diffusion (Zt​=exp(21​Xt∧T2​−21​(t∧T)−21​∫0t∧T​Xs2​ds))

Words: 90
Girsanov theorem OurBigBook.com
Under a reference measure where X is Brownian motion started at zero, let T be its exit time from (−1,1). The displayed density is the stochastic exponential with integrand X1[0,T]​, by the Itô formula. It is bounded by e1/2, hence defines a uniformly integrable density process with terminal density ZT​. Under that measure change, Xt​−∫0t∧T​Xs​ds is Brownian motion. At exit, ZT​≥e1/2−T, implying P(T≤t)≥e1/2−tP(T≤t). This is a terminal density on the whole probability space, not merely an unspecified finite-horizon change of measure.

Semimartingale invariance under equivalent measures

Words: 54
Girsanov theorem OurBigBook.com
On a fixed finite horizon, equivalent probability measures have the same semimartingales. For a strictly positive continuous Radon-Nikodym density martingale Z and a continuous local martingale L under the original measure, L−∫Z−1d[L,Z] is a local martingale under the new one, by the Girsanov theorem. Thus the finite-variation part of a continuous semimartingale decomposition changes by the opposite covariation correction.

Finite-horizon drift replacement by a change of measure

Words: 69
Girsanov theorem OurBigBook.com
For dX=μdt+σdB on [0,T], take θ=(ν−μ)/σ and use density E(∫θdB)T​. If μ,ν are bounded and σ is continuous and bounded below by a positive constant, the exponential has bounded bracket and defines an equivalent measure. Under it, B=B−∫θdt is Brownian and dX=νdt+σdB. Set θ=0 after T to define the density on the entire original sigma-algebra and the new Brownian motion on the whole time axis.

Girsanov density for a stopped Bessel process ((RT​/x)(δ−1)/2exp{−81​(δ−1)(δ−3)∫0T​Rs−2​ds})

Words: 164 Articles: 1
Girsanov theorem OurBigBook.com
For reference Brownian motion R=x+W, stopped at T=t∧τ(a,b)​ with 0<a<x<b, this expression is the Radon-Nikodym derivative of the stopped Bessel process law of dimension δ. The bounded stopped drift verifies the Novikov condition. The comparison laws must have the same initial value and the same stopping rule.
Brownian conditioning by a stopped Bessel density (L(RTM​)=Lx​(BTM​∣TM​<T0​))
Words: 121
Girsanov density for a stopped Bessel process OurBigBook.com
For 0<x<M, a three-dimensional Bessel process stopped at M has the law of Brownian motion conditioned to hit M before zero and stopped at M. On (ε,M), the Girsanov theorem and the Itô formula give terminal density Xτ​/x. Its value is M/x at the upper exit and ε/x at the lower exit. Letting ε↓0 in bounded stopped-path functionals gives density (M/x)1{TM​<T0​}​ relative to the corresponding stopped Wiener measure. The exit probability is x/M by the optional stopping theorem, so the density is normalized. On the unstopped full path space the same density defines the conditioned Brownian law; pushing it forward by the stopping map gives the stopped Bessel law. The already-stopped law is not absolutely continuous relative to unstopped Wiener measure, since eventually constant paths have Wiener probability zero.

Martingale transfer under a density process

Words: 184 Articles: 2
Girsanov theorem OurBigBook.com
Let Z be a positive uniformly integrable martingale defining dP=Z∞​dP. If Y is bounded and ZY is a true P-martingale, then Y is a P-martingale. This follows from the conditional-expectation change-of-measure identity.
Initial integrability under a density change (X0​∈L1(Q))
Words: 76
Martingale transfer under a density process OurBigBook.com
The density-product proof of the Girsanov theorem makes drift-corrected zero-starting increments a local martingale under the new measure. Adding the initial random variable requires its integrability under that measure. This is automatic if the density is one at time zero, because the measures agree on the initial sigma-algebra. Without this normalization it can fail: take P(n)=2−n, Q(n)=c/n2, constant Mt​=log(Q(n)/P(n)) and constant Xt​=n. These are P-martingales and the prescribed exponential density is valid, but X0​ is not Q-integrable.
Bounded-process density-product criterion
Words: 69
Martingale transfer under a density process OurBigBook.com
Let Z be a positive uniformly integrable density martingale. If Y is bounded and ZY is a local martingale under the original measure, the product is a true martingale: its stopped absolute values are dominated by a fixed multiple of the uniformly integrable stopped density. Bayes then makes Y a martingale under the new measure. Stop a locally bounded continuous Y at absolute-value levels to obtain the local version.
